identity.title: Progressive distillation induces an implicit curriculum

problem.claim: A better teacher does not consistently produce a better student in knowledge distillation.

contributions.claim: Identifies an implicit curriculum as a mechanism by which progressive distillation accelerates student learning in sparse parity.
Reports that the curriculum is present in intermediate teacher checkpoints but absent from the final converged checkpoint, with an associated provable sample-complexity benefit.
Extends the investigation to PCFG Transformers and Wikipedia and Books pre-training data, identifying progressive learning of longer-context features.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish progressive distillation by an implicit curriculum available through intermediate, but not final converged, checkpoints.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report empirical acceleration and a provable sample-complexity benefit for students receiving the intermediate-checkpoint curriculum in sparse parity.
The authors report an analogous curriculum in Transformers trained on PCFGs, characterized by progressively learned longer-context features.
The authors report empirical observations on Wikipedia and Books pre-training datasets consistent with benefits across setups.

narrative_sequence.summary: Knowledge distillation uses a teacher to improve a student, but teacher quality does not reliably translate into student quality.
Progressive distillation addresses this challenge by training from successive intermediate teacher checkpoints.
Sparse-parity analysis identifies an implicit curriculum that accelerates learning and provides a claimed sample-complexity benefit; it is unavailable from the final checkpoint alone.
Experiments on PCFG Transformers and Wikipedia and Books data probe a related curriculum in which longer-context features emerge progressively.
The authors present theoretical and empirical findings supporting benefits of progressive distillation via implicit curriculum across the studied setups.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a training procedure, the stage at which supervision is taken, and a specific mechanism—progressive acquisition of longer-context features—to reported learning benefits.

lessons.interpretation: A compact mechanism-centered framing can make a method claim more explanatory than reporting the procedure and outcome alone.
lessons.application: When presenting a staged training method, explicitly state which intermediate state supplies the signal, what representation or capability is acquired progressively, and which outcome is attributed to that mechanism.
lessons.exception: Do not use this framing when the mechanism is only hypothesized or when the abstract provides no evidence distinguishing it from alternative explanations.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative acceleration, sample-complexity bound, or baseline comparison.
Conditions and proof assumptions for the theoretical benefit are unspecified.
The scope and quantitative strength of the PCFG, Wikipedia, and Books observations are not reported.
